issues.legal_issue: A suit by a person claiming to be a licensee against an alleged licensor for an injunction protecting possession from threatened unlawful dispossession relates to recovery of possession and falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the designated small causes court when the property is within its territorial area.
material_facts: In both suits, the plaintiffs alleged that they occupied the premises under licences granted by the defendants and paid or were liable to pay consideration for those licences.
The plaintiffs sought injunctions to prevent the defendants from dispossessing them or interfering with their possession without due process of law.
The premises were immovable property within the relevant territorial area.
The court considered jurisdiction on the plaint allegations, taking them to be true, rather than deciding the parties’ competing claims on the merits.
issues.conclusion: The suits related to recovery of possession and could be entertained only by the Small Causes Court, not the City Civil Court. The appeals were dismissed, with the plaints to be returned for presentation to the proper court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, gives the Small Causes Court exclusive jurisdiction over suits between licensor and licensee relating to recovery of possession of immovable property within the specified area. The words “relating to” are broad and encompass an injunction suit seeking to prevent a licensor from forcibly recovering possession. The substance of the relief and the plaint allegations govern; a declaration of licensee status need not be separately sought. Section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act uses materially similar language. The Court relied on Renusagar Power Co. v. General Electric Co. for the broad meaning of “relating to,” Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for the breadth of related expressions, and Babulal Bhuramal v. Nandram Shivram and Natraj Studios v. Navrang Studios on suits concerning possession and exclusive jurisdiction. It also approved the same approach in Ambalal v. Narmada, Ramkishore v. Vijaybahadursingh, and Dattatreya Krishna v. Jairam Ganesh. A pure possessory suit of the kind contemplated by Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, stands on a different footing because the claimant need not establish a licensor-licensee relationship or title.

rule.if: licensee_injunction_suit and license_relationship_pleaded and property_within_forum_area and threatened_unlawful_dispossession

predicates.licensee_injunction_suit: A person claiming to occupy property as a licensee sues the alleged licensor for an injunction protecting possession.
predicates.license_relationship_pleaded: The claimant pleads a licensor-licensee relationship between the parties.
predicates.property_within_forum_area: The property is within the territorial area assigned to the specialized small causes court.
predicates.threatened_unlawful_dispossession: The claimant alleges that the licensor threatens to dispossess the claimant without following lawful process.

issues.definition: When a claimant pleads a licensee-injunction suit, a licensor-licensee relationship, property within the forum area, and threatened unlawful dispossession, the specialized small causes court has exclusive jurisdiction.
